We can introduce a new variable $z={n}^{3}$ and then rewrite the trinomial as a quadratic in terms of $n:$

$$
\begin{aligned}9{n}^{6}+6{n}^{3}+1 & =9{({n}^{3})}^{2}+6{n}^{3}+1 \\  & =9{z}^{2}+6z+1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can factor the quadratic as the square of a sum, and then rewrite the final expression in terms of $n:$

$$
\begin{aligned}9{z}^{2}+6z+1 & =(3z)^{2}+6z+1 \\  & ={(3z+1)}^{2} \\  & ={(3{n}^{3}+1)}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We can introduce a new variable $z=x^2$ and then rewrite the trinomial as a quadratic in terms of $z\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{4}-4{x}^{2}+4 & = \\ {({x}^{2})}^{2}-4({x}^{2})+4 & = \\ {z}^{2}-4z+4\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can factor the quadratic as the square of a difference, and then rewrite the final expression in terms of $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{z}^{2}-4z+4 & = \\ (z-2)^{2} & = \\ ({x}^{2}-2)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Suppose that we want to factor the following trinomial:

$$
t^4+4t^2+3.
$$

This trinomial is a quartic, but it can also be viewed as a quadratic "in disguise." To see this, notice that if we introduce a new variable $z=t^2,$ then we can rewrite the trinomial as a quadratic in terms of $z\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{4}+4{t}^{2}+3 & = \\ ({t}^{2})^{2}+4({t}^{2})+3 & = \\ {z}^{2}+4z+3\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can factor the quadratic, and then rewrite the final expression in terms of $t\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{z}^{2}+4z+3 & = \\ (z+1)(z+3) & = \\ ({t}^{2}+1)({t}^{2}+3)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $t^4+4t^2+3$ factors into $(t^2+1)(t^2+3).$ We can double-check this result by multiplying it out:

$$
\begin{aligned}({t}^{2}+1)({t}^{2}+3) & = \\ {t}^{2}({t}^{2}+3)+1({t}^{2}+3) & = \\ {t}^{4}+3{t}^{2}+{t}^{2}+3 & = \\ {t}^{4}+4{t}^{2}+3 & \,✓\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.content:
Suppose that we want to factor the following trinomial:

$$
t^4+4t^2+3.
$$

This trinomial is a quartic, but it can also be viewed as a quadratic "in disguise." To see this, notice that if we introduce a new variable $z=t^2,$ then we can rewrite the trinomial as a quadratic in terms of $z\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{4}+4{t}^{2}+3 & = \\ ({t}^{2})^{2}+4({t}^{2})+3 & = \\ {z}^{2}+4z+3\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can factor the quadratic, and then rewrite the final expression in terms of $t\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{z}^{2}+4z+3 & = \\ (z+1)(z+3) & = \\ ({t}^{2}+1)({t}^{2}+3)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $t^4+4t^2+3$ factors into $(t^2+1)(t^2+3).$ We can double-check this result by multiplying it out:

$$
\begin{aligned}({t}^{2}+1)({t}^{2}+3) & = \\ {t}^{2}({t}^{2}+3)+1({t}^{2}+3) & = \\ {t}^{4}+3{t}^{2}+{t}^{2}+3 & = \\ {t}^{4}+4{t}^{2}+3 & \,✓\end{aligned}
$$
